thread_title: S. flava var. rubricorpora Bay County, FL 2014
breadcrumb: S. flava var. rubricorpora Bay County, FL 2014

posts.body_html:
It doesn't take a rocket scientist to know that one of the best S. flava var. rubricorpora populations in the world still exists today in Bay County, FL. Apparently, it does take a genius to explain to the State of Florida that destroying this remaining habitat and not having regulations to protect the remaining sites is beyond ridiculous, seeing how they've already demolished literally everything they possibly could.

Bay County encompasses 1,033 sq miles (2,675 km²), and out of all of that land, maybe 10-20 acres of pristine habitat is left. Most of the remaining sites are relic patches of once vast fields of dreams. One can only imagine how many endless acres of fields filled with red flavas once existed.

Everything that is left in the wild in Bay County is surrounded by altered terrain or is altered terrain. I visited a site in 2011 that was reported to have huge fields of Sarracenias and natural ponds containing giant floating S. psittacinas! Can you guess what this site looks like today? It looks like what 90% of Bay County looks like: endless rows of non-native pines grown for pulp production! No ponds, no savannas, no rare native plants, no sunshine, just thick, dark forests of planted trees as far as the eye can see. Unlike us CP enthusiasts, the majority of the general public sees nothing wrong with this: after all, they've "reforested America"!

To add insult to injury, one of the last remaining sites is literally on it's last legs: the parcel right next to the red flava site, which is slightly uphill and is the water source for the delicate savanna, was recently harvested and cleared but fortunately, much of the soil was left undisturbed. Will they come in with tractors and till the soil to plant more trees? Will they dig ditches and destroy the water table? Keep in mind, many of these springs are extremely shallow. Even without laying a finger on the savanna, this site can be destroyed by altering the neighboring land.

Well, the rest of the story has yet to be written, but there is hope that fields like these will keep going past our time. After all, this site still does exist as of 2014, and it's THRIVING! I'm grateful we live in a time when there's still pitcher plants in the wild, and it's a pleasure to share this with you all.


Try to imagine the most amazing, giant, diverse red tubed plants you've ever seen, and that's what's here, in relatively large numbers. Also try to imagine 99F (37C) weather that felt like 110F (43C) and mosquitoes and other insects constantly biting you while you're drenched in sweat. Oh, and when you step on a little spot of dry land in the bog, it's infested with ants that bite with a painful sting (yes, I got bit!):



When we visited, the field was very mucky and wet, so walking around was quite difficult. The insects trying to eat you alive wasn't any help either. Let me also mention that most other sites we visited in Florida this time of the year were bone dry and had a lot less biting insects! Every step, your foot goes down 2-3 ft (almost a meter deep). I ended up walking barefoot:



I couldn't figure out if this site is being burned, but it didn't seem so. While the grasses were pretty thick in some areas, the field was so boggy and wet that not much else was colonizing the field. Anywhere else, this would be a thick forest within 2-3 years, things grow very fast in Florida:



Each individual plant produced one or two pitchers, and not too many plants seemed to form clumps despite being well spaced and in full sun:



Most of the plants here were red tubes, but some were extreme red throats. I didn't see any plants that resembled "pure" S. flava var. rugelii:



Some more habitat shots:





And now for some closer shots. Look at the character on these traps!



Some of the lids stay yellow-green even after they age:



Like this one too, and check out how big the lid is:



Bright red body:



Standard looking giant trap, hard to tell from the photo just how big these are:





Some outstanding individuals:



It's hard to capture the real color of these traps, but this picture is spot on. The light just happened to be perfect:



One last look at the field as we exited. Wish I snapped more photos, but we were tired, hungry, bitten, dehydrated, and overheated, so it was time to go:


After a long day of bogging, to relieve our bug bites and relax our bones, we went for a dip in the pool with some odd rules(item#7):


Well, that's it for the story of the red tube site, hope you enjoyed it!

Mike, terrific post. Your intro is written so well the issues you highlight are easily consumable. By all The Gods let's hope time marches in Sarracenia's favour in these areas. I thought your point on the public reacting positively to the pine plantations was an insightful one. A diabolical, but fully understandable quandary when it comes to Sarracenia public relations which sound as though, outside of us types, are relatively non-existent. I know you are putting a significant amount of energy into finding ways of addressing these issues. More power to you.

Thanks so much for making the images of this enigmatic site available to we that live so far away. What a fascinating place.

I guess its no surprise when I say the fact that each plant produces very few pitchers is notable: a classic rubricorpora trait throughout that variety's colour spectrum.

And, that pool sign? What a laugh! "Bathing Load". What a quaint term.

posts.body_html:
Finally managing to get some posts together from this season's two awesome bog trips. These photos were taken May 10, 2015 on DirtyDivisions and my "early season" trip. On this day we were very fortunate to visit one of the last remaining populations of S. flava in Bay Co - I think the number of viable populations as of 2015 doesn't take up all the fingers on one hand, sad to say. That said, this bog appears to be thriving. It's water supply is abundant (to say the least!), supporting a diverse population of flavas and some of the biggest S. psittacina EVAR, and making it virtually impossible to plant the spot with pine trees as the entire surrounding area already has been. Interestingly, the pine plantation on one side of the bog was harvested recently and some expressed concern that this disturbance might alter the hydrology of the bog for the worse. I am happy to report that this has not occurred and that the bog is as boot-swallowingly mucky as ever. In fact, clearing all those thirsty trees from part of the water recharge zone probably leaves more water for the bog!

On to the plants. meizzwang 's excellent posts on this site made us very excited to visit. His photos taken in the late season clearly show that by September or so most plants at this site have infused solid red and look like "atropurpureas." Since this also occurs at the famous Liberty Co. red tube site, Trey and I expected to find a population of plants looking broadly similar to the Liberty Co. flavas: red or mostly red bodies with green lids, and some ornata and "atropurpurea" outliers. Well folks we were in for a surprise! The plants at this site are mostly green in the early season! Here is an overview of a representative sample:

At this time of year the plants were mostly ornatas with a redder plant standing out here and there. These are typical:


Cool hunting spider:

Some had a bit more red at this stage:


There were many stunning "extreme red throat" plants here as well.


As an aside: before Mike coined the ERT name, these plants were casually called "ornata" - a good example of how "var. ornata" has become a catch-all category for anything odd that displays the inadequacy and incompleteness of the other existing varieties. There are many such plants in wild populations: just go to Okaloosa Co! I think it's funny that we are back to the pre-1998 situation of creating informal names to attempt to describe the diversity in wild S. flava. Don S. better catch up! Perhaps he is working on descriptions of several new varieties now...
Yet another interesting thing about this site and the ERT genetics is the conspicuous absence of var. rugelii. I think we spotted ONE small rugelii plant in the whole place and this was the only site we saw in the whole Panhandle where this color form was so rare. Most of the ornatas here lacked rugelii-style throat blotches as well, with the ERT form being the dominant manifestation of throat blotching. A Gulf Coast flava population with minimal rugelii influence?? These genetics are SO WEIRD.
On to the red plants! To reiterate, these plants were a tiny minority within the population at the time of our visit. They do look remarkably similar in color to the Liberty Co. plants however. 
[URL=http://s1329.photobucket.com/user/calenhall/media/image.jpg7_zps6hevoxfs.jpg.ht[/URL]


Gotta repost this crazy muggafugga:

I have no doubt that most of the veined plants will color quite strongly after several months of exposure, but we were pretty flabbergasted at the contrast with the Liberty Co. plants. The latter definitely darken considerably after opening, but the "typical" individual has a red tube before or at the time the traps open. The color behavior of the Bay Co. plants reminds me of S. alata in which even plants that age solid red open with lightly veined green tubes. Early season photos I have seen from the huge Stone Co. MS site famous for its red alatas contain not a single visible red plant! By mid-summer however the field has countless red plants. This behavior definitely throws a wrench in the color variety scheme as it is currently accepted. As others have asked, how can a plant be variety A in May, variety B in July, and then variety C in September? Do our concepts of color variation in S. flava match reality on the ground in wild populations? Does a sensible way to divide the color diversity in S. flava into separate categories even exist? And if it does, is it important to do so? Look for more fuel on this fire from what Trey and I saw in Okaloosa Co. this season...

posts.body_html:
That looks Super Bawgy Calen! No idea how you guys walked through that site...it was pretty darn impossible to navigate when it was a lot drier last fall. Anyhow, thanks for documenting this significant observation, absolutely unexpected and crazy to see the field practically greenish!

I think I sent Donny Schnell an ERT and I'm pretty darn sure he's been to this site, so hopefully if he isn't already making some amendments, he's at least seeing what we see: a completely different variant. I'm doing an experiment with ERT's and some ornatas to see if they breed true. My guess is that you'll see the same thing you see with rubricorporas: whether or not they breed true depends on the genetics of the parents.

Last random thought: I wish there was some way to get a sense of just how enormous those pitchers are...they're way bigger in reality compared to how they appear in the pix.
